hook: The great Mughal emperor who could not read, and welcomed every religion to his court.

pages.x: Akbar was born in 1542 at Umarkot, in Sindh, while his father, the Mughal emperor Humayun, was on the run after losing his throne. Humayun won it back, but in 1556 he fell down the stairs of his library and died. Akbar became emperor at 13.
Within weeks a Hindu general, Hemu, seized Delhi. At the Second Battle of Panipat in 1556 an arrow struck Hemu in the eye, his army broke, and the young Mughal empire was saved.

pages.t: The emperor who could not read
pages.x: Akbar never learned to read, perhaps because he was dyslexic, but he built a library of 24,000 books and had them read aloud to him, remembering everything. He loved hunting with tame cheetahs, and riding war elephants.
He won over the proud Rajput kings by marriage and alliance, and ended the tax that non-Muslims had to pay. Hindus became his generals and ministers. His empire grew to cover most of northern India.
He built a new capital of red sandstone near Agra, Fatehpur Sikri, with a victory gate 54 metres high. It was abandoned after only about 14 years, perhaps because it ran short of water.

In his House of Worship he invited Sunni and Shia scholars, Hindus, Jains, Zoroastrians and Jesuit priests to debate their faiths in front of him. He later started a faith of his own, the "divine faith", which had only a handful of followers.

His witty minister Birbal is the hero of hundreds of Indian folk tales. In one, Akbar draws a line and asks his courtiers to make it shorter without touching it. Birbal simply draws a longer line beside it.
Akbar made the Mughal Empire one of the richest states on Earth and ruled it with a tolerance rare in his time. Indians still call him Akbar the Great.
pts: Spread the Mughal Empire across northern India
Ruled with tolerance for all religions
